record.paper_title: Recent Results and Open Problems in Evolutionary Multiobjective Optimization
record.original_question: For expensive multi-objective optimization problems, where objective-function evaluations are costly, how can fitness approximation and surrogate modeling be incorporated into multi-objective evolutionary algorithms so that fewer true objective evaluations are needed without losing reliable approximation of the Pareto front?

evidence.quote: Taking this to the multiobjective case is not trivial
The implementation of MOEAs that incorporate surrogate methods is not trivial!

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a multi-objective optimization problem of the form: minimize F(x) = (f_1(x), ..., f_m(x)) over x in a feasible domain X ⊂ R^n, where m ≥ 2 and each objective evaluation f_i(x) is computationally expensive (e.g., requires running a costly simulation). A point x* is Pareto-optimal if there is no x in X with f_i(x) ≤ f_i(x*) for all i and f_j(x) < f_j(x*) for some j; the Pareto front is the image of the set of Pareto-optimal points under F. A multi-objective evolutionary algorithm (MOEA) is a population-based stochastic search procedure that maintains and evolves a finite set of candidate solutions through variation (crossover, mutation) and selection operators to approximate the Pareto front. A fitness approximation or surrogate model is a computationally cheap function F̂(x) (for instance a Kriging/Gaussian-process model, radial basis function network, polynomial response surface, or neural network) trained on a sample of true evaluations and used as a proxy for F during parts of the search.

Develop a principled framework for incorporating surrogate models into MOEAs for such expensive multi-objective problems. Specifically:
(a) Define how to construct, update, and manage one or several surrogate models for the m objectives (e.g., one surrogate per objective, a single aggregated surrogate, or models for scalarized sub-problems), addressing the curse of dimensionality in both n and m.
(b) Specify an infill / model-management strategy that decides which candidate solutions are evaluated by the true (expensive) F and which only by F̂, so as to balance exploration and exploitation across the Pareto front.
(c) Provide theoretical or empirical guarantees that, under a fixed budget of true evaluations, the resulting algorithm produces an approximation of the Pareto front (measured by indicators such as hypervolume, generational distance, or inverted generational distance) that is competitive with, and ideally provably converges to, the true Pareto front as the budget grows, while requiring substantially fewer true objective evaluations than a non-surrogate MOEA.

Resolve these three points jointly to give a complete, justified methodology for surrogate-assisted multi-objective evolutionary optimization of expensive objectives.
artifact.status_search_result: Surrogate-assisted MOEAs constitute an active and rapidly growing research area; numerous methods (e.g., ParEGO, MOEA/D-EGO, K-RVEA, CSEA, HeE-MOEA) have been proposed, but there is no single canonical framework, and central questions about scalability to many objectives, model-management strategies, and convergence guarantees remain open as of 2026. Recent surveys describe the topic as an ongoing open challenge rather than a solved problem.

status_evidence.title: A Survey on Surrogate-Assisted Evolutionary Algorithms for Expensive Optimization
status_evidence.snippet: Identifies surrogate-assisted MOEAs for expensive multi-objective problems as an active research area with open issues in many-objective scaling and model management.
status_evidence.claim: Topic is surveyed as ongoing with open challenges.

status_evidence.title: Recent advances in surrogate-assisted evolutionary multi/many-objective optimization
status_evidence.snippet: Reviews state-of-the-art SAEAs for expensive MOPs and lists outstanding open problems including high-dimensional surrogates and infill criteria.
status_evidence.claim: Authors explicitly list open problems in this area.
